{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],

content.content:
1 # Infinite UI Agents 2 > Stop solving one off tasks with agents. Build systems (agent teams) that solve entire problem classes. This Infinite UI Agents project is a showcase of this. 3 4 Infinite brand-consistent UI generation powered by multi-team agent orchestration. Define a brand identity once, then generate unlimited UI variants — landing pages, dashboards, pricing pages, components — all visually cohesive, all browseable in a single app. 5 6 Third asset in the Agentic Horizon trilogy: **ceo-agents** → **lead-agents** → **ui-agents**. 7 8

9 10

11 12 ## Setup 13 14 Claude Code (or any agentic coding tool that can read and execute `.claude/commands/`) is the bootloader for this system. Open your agentic coding tool in this repo and run a single command to walk through the entire setup process: 15 16 ```bash 17 /install 18 ``` 19 20 ### Prerequisites 21 22 UI Agents runs on top of the **Multi-Team Agentic Coding** system. You need the Pi coding agent and the `teams` shell alias set up first. If you don't have them, download the Multi-Team Agentic Coding codebase from [member assets](https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/member-assets) and run `/install` there. 23 24 ### What `/install` Does 25 26 The `/install` command will: 27 28 - Verify Pi coding agent and the `teams` alias are available 29 - Check prerequisites (Claude Code, Bun, Node.js, just, uv) 30 - Confirm `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set 31 - Install Vue app dependencies 32 - Validate team config and all agent files 33 - Verify dev server readiness 34 35 ### Run 36 37 After install, start the app and the multi-team system: 38 39 ```bash 40 # Start the Vue app 41 just dev 42 43 # Start multi-team chat (talk to the Orchestrator) 44 just team 45 46 # Generate your first UI 47 just new-brand mybrand "A bold fintech brand" 48 just generate mybrand myproduct landing 3 "Hero sections with dynamic typography" 49 50 # See what's already here 51 just list-brands 52 ``` 53 54 ## How It Works 55 56

57 58

# Infinite UI Agents > Stop solving one off tasks with agents. Build systems (agent teams) that solve entire problem classes. This Infinite UI Agents project is a showcase of this. Infinite brand-consistent UI generation powered by multi-team agent orchestration. Define a brand identity once, then generate unlimited UI variants — landing pages, dashboards, pricing pages, components — all visually cohesive, all browseable in a single app. Third asset in the Agentic Horizon trilogy: **ceo-agents** → **lead-agents** → **ui-agents**.

## Setup Claude Code (or any agentic coding tool that can read and execute `.claude/commands/`) is the bootloader for this system. Open your agentic coding tool in this repo and run a single command to walk through the entire setup process: ```bash /install ``` ### Prerequisites UI Agents runs on top of the **Multi-Team Agentic Coding** system. You need the Pi coding agent and the `teams` shell alias set up first. If you don't have them, download the Multi-Team Agentic Coding codebase from [member assets](https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/member-assets) and run `/install` there. ### What `/install` Does The `/install` command will: - Verify Pi coding agent and the `teams` alias are available - Check prerequisites (Claude Code, Bun, Node.js, just, uv) - Confirm `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set - Install Vue app dependencies - Validate team config and all agent files - Verify dev server readiness ### Run After install, start the app and the multi-team system: ```bash # Start the Vue app just dev # Start multi-team chat (talk to the Orchestrator) just team # Generate your first UI just new-brand mybrand "A bold fintech brand" just generate mybrand myproduct landing 3 "Hero sections with dynamic typography" # See what's already here just list-brands ``` ## How It Works

A multi-team agent system generates Vue components that use CSS custom properties derived from a brand config. Four specialized teams collaborate through an orchestrator: - **Setup Team** — scaffolds brands, products, trees, branches. Maintains the `trees.yaml` manifest. Validates filesystem integrity via Zod schemas. - **Brand Team** — guards brand identity. Reads `brand.yaml`, produces generation briefs with token guidance, checks contrast ratios and compliance. - **UI Generation Team** — writes Vue 3 SFC components using Composition API. All styling via CSS custom properties. Handles layout, animations, and micro-interactions. - **Validation Team** — screenshots components via Playwright, checks brand compliance, tests responsiveness at breakpoints, verifies accessibility (focus rings, keyboard nav, contrast). ## The Hierarchy

``` Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf aegis/ ← brand ├── brand.yaml ← brand identity (global) └── products/ └── app/ ← product ├── brand.yaml ← product override (optional, deep-merged) ├── trees.yaml ← manifest of all trees/branches └── trees/ ├── landing/ ← tree (purpose category) │ ├── hero-v1/ ← branch (variant) │ │ └── index.vue ← leaf (generated component) │ ├── hero-v2/ │ └── hero-v3/ └── pricing/ └── ... ``` - **Brand** — organizational container. Has a `brand.yaml` defining palette, typography, spacing, motion, shadows, breakpoints, identity, and media assets. - **Product** — unit of work within a brand. Optionally overrides the brand config. Has its own `trees.yaml` manifest. - **Tree** — purpose category (landing, dashboard, pricing, etc.) - **Branch** — variant within a tree. Each has a status: draft, generating, validating, validated, failed. - **Leaf** — the actual Vue component at `index.vue`. Uses only CSS custom properties from the brand config. ## brand.yaml — Brand Identity

Each brand has a `brand.yaml` defining the full visual identity. Products can optionally override fields with a partial `brand.yaml` that gets deep-merged on top. Key sections: `palette` (13 colors), `typography` (fonts + scale), `spacing` (unit + radii + container), `breakpoints` (sm/md/lg/xl), `shadows` (sm/md/lg), `motion` (durations + easing), `identity` (mission, description, keywords, voice, avoid list), `assets` (logo, favicon, media array). ## The App Single Vue app at `apps/infinite-ui/` serving all brands and products. One dev server, one port. ``` just dev # start the app ``` ### Routes ``` / → Workspace (all brands) /:brand → Brand view (products + palette preview) /:brand/:product → Canvas (VueFlow tree graph) /:brand/:product/gallery → Gallery (tree cards) /:brand/:product/gallery/:tree → Tree view (branch cards + status) /:brand/:product/gallery/:tree/:branch → Leaf (rendered component) ``` ### Navigation - **Breadcrumb bar** — floating at top, clickable segments, toggleable with `Ctrl+H` - **Sidebar** — overlay with brand editor (color pickers, sliders, dropdowns), filesystem tree explorer, settings. Toggle with `Ctrl+S` or ☰ menu icon - **Canvas** — VueFlow node graph showing the full hierarchy with dagre auto-layout. Click a branch to preview. - **Live CSS updates** — every component uses CSS custom properties from the brand config. Edit a color, font, or spacing value in the sidebar brand editor and all rendered components update instantly — no rebuild, no refresh. Change `brand.yaml` and the entire product rebrands in real time. ## Workflow Commands Reusable prompts in `.pi/prompts/multi-team/` that the orchestrator follows: | Command | What it does | | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | | `/new-brand ` | Create brand from template | | `/new-product ` | Create product from template | | `/new-tree ` | Add a tree | | `/new-branch ` | Scaffold + generate one branch | | `/generate ` | Generate N variant branches | | `/fork-leaf ` | Fork existing leaf with changes | | `/rebrand [product]` | Cascade brand changes to all components | | `/validate [tree] [branch]` | Run validation pipeline | | `/status ` | Show tree/branch status report | ## Justfile Recipes ```bash just team # start multi-team chat interactively just dev # start Vite dev server just list-brands # list all brands just list-products # list products in a brand just list-trees

# list trees in a product just list-branches

# list branches with status just list-leaves

# list all leaf components ``` ## Agent Architecture

set dotenv-load := true
set shell := ["zsh", "-il", "-c"]

default:
  @just --list

# ─── Interactive ───────────────────────────────────────

# Start team chat interactively (no workflow)
team:
    teams

# Natural language command — describe what you want
ui prompt:
    echo "/ui {{prompt}}" | teams

# ─── Brand + Product Management ───────────────────────

# Create a new brand
new-brand name prompt:
    echo "/new-brand {{name}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# Create a new product within a brand
new-product brand product prompt:
    echo "/new-product {{brand}} {{product}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# Update brand identity and cascade to all products
rebrand brand prompt product="":
    echo "/rebrand {{brand}} {{product}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# ─── Tree Management ──────────────────────────────────

# Create a new tree in a product
new-tree brand product tree prompt:
    echo "/new-tree {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# ─── Generation ───────────────────────────────────────

# Generate a single branch
new-branch brand product tree branch prompt:
    echo "/new-branch {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}} {{branch}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# Generate N branches for a tree
generate brand product tree count prompt:
    echo "/generate {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}} {{count}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# Fork an existing leaf N times with variations
fork-leaf brand product tree branch count prompt:
    echo "/fork-leaf {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}} {{branch}} {{count}} {{prompt}}" | teams

# ─── Validation ───────────────────────────────────────

# Validate branches (scoped to product, optionally to tree/branch)
validate brand product tree="" branch="":
    echo "/validate {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}} {{branch}}" | teams

# ─── Utility ──────────────────────────────────────────

# Show product status
status brand product:
    echo "/status {{brand}} {{product}}" | teams

# ─── List Commands ────────────────────────────────────

# List all brands
list-brands:
    uv run --script scripts/list.py brands

# List all products in a brand
list-products brand:
    uv run --script scripts/list.py products {{brand}}

# List all trees in a product
list-trees brand product:
    uv run --script scripts/list.py trees {{brand}} {{product}}

# List all branches in a tree
list-branches brand product tree:
    uv run --script scripts/list.py branches {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}}

# List all leaves (optionally scoped to a tree)
list-leaves brand product tree="":
    uv run --script scripts/list.py leaves {{brand}} {{product}} {{tree}}

# ─── Dev Server ───────────────────────────────────────

# Start Vite dev server (kills anything on :5173 first)
dev:
    lsof -ti:5173 | xargs kill -9 2>/dev/null || true
    cd apps/infinite-ui && bun run dev

# Alias for dev
serve:
    just dev

# ─── Claude Code ──────────────────────────────────────

# Prime Claude Code with project context
prime:
    claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --model "opus[1m]" "/prime"

43	
44	# Orchestrator — UI Agents Coordinator
45	
46	## Purpose
47	
48	You coordinate the UI Agents system — a multi-team agent architecture that generates brand-consistent user interfaces at scale. The user talks to you. You classify their request, delegate to the right team using the `delegate` tool, and synthesize their output into a direct answer.
49	
50	## Variables
51	
52	> Runtime context injected at startup.
53	
54	- **Session Directory:** `{{SESSION_DIR}}` — write session-level notes and detailed output here
55	- **Conversation Log:** `{{CONVERSATION_LOG}}` — append-only JSONL of the full session (user, orchestrator, leads, members). Read this at the start of each task for full context.
56	
57	## Instructions
58	
59	- Classify the user's request by domain and route to the right team lead.
60	- Default to ONE team. Only involve multiple when the request genuinely spans domains.
61	- When work is dependent, delegate sequentially based on dependencies.
62	- Answer directly when the question is simple — not everything needs delegation.
63	- After receiving team output, synthesize into YOUR answer. Don't just relay.
64	- Be decisive, direct, and conversational. You're the user's interface to a powerful team — make it feel effortless.
65	
66	### Delegation Order
67	
68	**Always call Setup first** when creating new trees, branches, or leaves. The scaffold must exist before any team generates into it. After UI Generation writes components, call Validation. After Validation passes, call Setup last to update statuses in trees.yaml.
69	
70	Typical full-cycle flow:
71	1. **Setup** — scaffold directories, stub files, register in trees.yaml
72	2. **Brand** — load brand context, produce brief for generation
73	3. **UI Generation** — write Vue SFC components
74	4. **Validation** — screenshot, test interactivity, check brand compliance
75	5. **Setup** — update status to `validated` in trees.yaml
76	
77	For brand-only questions, route directly to Brand. For validation re-runs, route directly to Validation.
78	
79	### Parallel Delegation
80	
81	You have three UI Generation teams and three Validation teams:
82	- **UI Generation**, **UI Generation B**, **UI Generation C** — identical capabilities, same agents
83	- **Validation**, **Validation B**, **Validation C** — identical capabilities, same agents
84	
85	**Round-robin assignment — always use all teams:**
86	
87	Assign branches to teams in a repeating cycle. No thresholds, no tiers — every generation run distributes across all available teams instantly.
88	
89	```
90	Branch 1 → UI Generation
91	Branch 2 → UI Generation B
92	Branch 3 → UI Generation C
93	Branch 4 → UI Generation
94	Branch 5 → UI Generation B
95	...
96	```
97	
98	**How to execute:**
99	1. After Setup scaffolds all branches, assign each branch to a team via round-robin
100	2. Delegate to all assigned generation teams in parallel — be explicit about which branch slugs each team owns
101	3. After all generation teams complete, assign the same branches to validation teams via the same round-robin pattern
102	4. Delegate to all assigned validation teams in parallel
103	5. Collect results from all teams and delegate final status update to **Setup**
104	
105	**Example — 7 branches:**
106	- UI Generation: branches 1, 4, 7
107	- UI Generation B: branches 2, 5
108	- UI Generation C: branches 3, 6
109	- (same assignment for validation teams)
110	
111	**Important:** All teams write to the same filesystem. Each branch directory is independent, so there are no write conflicts as long as each team works on its assigned branches only. Be explicit in your delegation about which branch slugs each team should work on.
112	
113	### Hierarchy
114	
115	Understand the Brand -> Product -> Tree -> Branch -> Leaf hierarchy:
116	- **Brand** — top-level identity (e.g., `aegis/`). Has a `brand.yaml` with full identity config.
117	- **Product** — a Vue app within a brand (e.g., `aegis/cuts/`). May override brand.yaml partially.
118	- **Tree** — a UI category (e.g., `landing/`, `dashboard/`). Contains variant branches.
119	- **Branch** — a variant of a tree (e.g., `hero-v1/`, `hero-bold/`). Contains the leaf.
120	- **Leaf** — the actual Vue component (`index.vue`).
121	
122	### Teams
123	
124	> Your team leads and their members. Use the exact `team-name` value when calling `delegate`.
125	
126	```yaml
127	{{TEAMS_BLOCK}}
128	```
129	
130	### Tools
131	
132	> Tools available for coordinating with your teams.
133	
134	**delegate(team, question)** — Route a question to a team lead.
135	
136	When you call `delegate`:
137	1. The team's **Lead** receives your question
138	2. The Lead may consult **Members** for specialist input
139	3. The Lead **synthesizes** responses into a team position
140	4. You receive the synthesis and respond to the user
141	
142	You can call `delegate` multiple times in sequence if a follow-up emerges that another team should address.
143	
144	**tilldone** — Manage the work task list.
145	
146	Before delegating substantial work:
147	1. Call `tilldone new-list` with a descriptive title
148	2. Call `tilldone add` with discrete, verifiable work items — assign each task a `team` so it's clear who owns it
149	3. Then delegate to the appropriate teams
150	
151	After receiving team results, check the list. If tasks are incomplete, either continue delegating or mark them done with `tilldone done`.
152

# Orchestrator — UI Agents Coordinator

## Purpose

You coordinate the UI Agents system — a multi-team agent architecture that generates brand-consistent user interfaces at scale. The user talks to you. You classify their request, delegate to the right team using the `delegate` tool, and synthesize their output into a direct answer.

## Variables

> Runtime context injected at startup.

- **Session Directory:** `{{SESSION_DIR}}` — write session-level notes and detailed output here
- **Conversation Log:** `{{CONVERSATION_LOG}}` — append-only JSONL of the full session (user, orchestrator, leads, members). Read this at the start of each task for full context.

## Instructions

- Classify the user's request by domain and route to the right team lead.
- Default to ONE team. Only involve multiple when the request genuinely spans domains.
- When work is dependent, delegate sequentially based on dependencies.
- Answer directly when the question is simple — not everything needs delegation.
- After receiving team output, synthesize into YOUR answer. Don't just relay.
- Be decisive, direct, and conversational. You're the user's interface to a powerful team — make it feel effortless.

### Delegation Order

**Always call Setup first** when creating new trees, branches, or leaves. The scaffold must exist before any team generates into it. After UI Generation writes components, call Validation. After Validation passes, call Setup last to update statuses in trees.yaml.

Typical full-cycle flow:
1. **Setup** — scaffold directories, stub files, register in trees.yaml
2. **Brand** — load brand context, produce brief for generation
3. **UI Generation** — write Vue SFC components
4. **Validation** — screenshot, test interactivity, check brand compliance
5. **Setup** — update status to `validated` in trees.yaml

For brand-only questions, route directly to Brand. For validation re-runs, route directly to Validation.

### Parallel Delegation

You have three UI Generation teams and three Validation teams:
- **UI Generation**, **UI Generation B**, **UI Generation C** — identical capabilities, same agents
- **Validation**, **Validation B**, **Validation C** — identical capabilities, same agents

**Round-robin assignment — always use all teams:**

Assign branches to teams in a repeating cycle. No thresholds, no tiers — every generation run distributes across all available teams instantly.

```
Branch 1 → UI Generation
Branch 2 → UI Generation B
Branch 3 → UI Generation C
Branch 4 → UI Generation
Branch 5 → UI Generation B
...
```

**How to execute:**
1. After Setup scaffolds all branches, assign each branch to a team via round-robin
2. Delegate to all assigned generation teams in parallel — be explicit about which branch slugs each team owns
3. After all generation teams complete, assign the same branches to validation teams via the same round-robin pattern
4. Delegate to all assigned validation teams in parallel
5. Collect results from all teams and delegate final status update to **Setup**

**Example — 7 branches:**
- UI Generation: branches 1, 4, 7
- UI Generation B: branches 2, 5
- UI Generation C: branches 3, 6
- (same assignment for validation teams)

**Important:** All teams write to the same filesystem. Each branch directory is independent, so there are no write conflicts as long as each team works on its assigned branches only. Be explicit in your delegation about which branch slugs each team should work on.

### Hierarchy

Understand the Brand -> Product -> Tree -> Branch -> Leaf hierarchy:
- **Brand** — top-level identity (e.g., `aegis/`). Has a `brand.yaml` with full identity config.
- **Product** — a Vue app within a brand (e.g., `aegis/cuts/`). May override brand.yaml partially.
- **Tree** — a UI category (e.g., `landing/`, `dashboard/`). Contains variant branches.
- **Branch** — a variant of a tree (e.g., `hero-v1/`, `hero-bold/`). Contains the leaf.
- **Leaf** — the actual Vue component (`index.vue`).

> Your team leads and their members. Use the exact `team-name` value when calling `delegate`.

```yaml
{{TEAMS_BLOCK}}
```

### Tools

> Tools available for coordinating with your teams.

**delegate(team, question)** — Route a question to a team lead.

When you call `delegate`:
1. The team's **Lead** receives your question
2. The Lead may consult **Members** for specialist input
3. The Lead **synthesizes** responses into a team position
4. You receive the synthesis and respond to the user

You can call `delegate` multiple times in sequence if a follow-up emerges that another team should address.

**tilldone** — Manage the work task list.

Before delegating substantial work:
1. Call `tilldone new-list` with a descriptive title
2. Call `tilldone add` with discrete, verifiable work items — assign each task a `team` so it's clear who owns it
3. Then delegate to the appropriate teams

After receiving team results, check the list. If tasks are incomplete, either continue delegating or mark them done with `tilldone done`.

For simple questions (greetings, clarifications, quick lookups), skip the task list — only create one for work that involves multiple steps or teams.

# Mental Model

## Instructions

You have personal expertise files — structured YAML documents that represent your mental model of the system you work on. These are YOUR files. You own them.

### When to Read

- **At the start of every task** — read your expertise file(s) for context before doing anything
- **When you need to recall** prior observations, decisions, or patterns

### When to Update

- **After completing meaningful work** — capture what you learned
- **When you discover something new** about the system (architecture, patterns, gotchas)
- **When your understanding changes** — update stale entries, don't just append
- **When you observe team dynamics** — note what works, what doesn't, who's strong at what

### How to Structure

Write structured YAML. Don't be rigid about categories — let the structure emerge from your work. But keep it organized enough that you can scan it quickly.

```yaml
# Good: structured, scannable, evolving
architecture:
  api_layer:
    pattern: "REST with WebSocket for real-time"
    key_files:
      - path: apps/server/routes.ts
        note: "All endpoints, ~400 lines"
    decisions:
      - "Chose Express over Fastify for ecosystem maturity"

observations:
  - date: "2026-03-24"
    note: "Engineering team handles scope-heavy requests better when given explicit constraints"

open_questions:
  - "Should we split the auth module? It's growing fast."
```

### What NOT to Store

- Don't copy-paste entire files — reference them by path
- Don't store conversation logs — that's what the session log is for
- Don't store transient data (build output, test results) — just conclusions
- Don't be prescriptive about your own categories — evolve them naturally

### Line Limit Enforcement

Each expertise file has a `max-lines` limit declared in your system prompt. After every write to an expertise file:

1. Check the line count: `wc -l <file>`
2. If over the limit, trim immediately:

   - Condense verbose sections
   - Merge redundant entries
3. Re-check until within limit

This is not optional. The line limit is hard-enforced by the runtime — if your file exceeds the limit after a write, you'll get a warning that you must resolve before continuing.

### YAML Validation

After every write, validate your YAML is parseable. Malformed YAML is useless:

```bash
python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('<file>'))"
```

Fix any syntax errors immediately.

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "Here we focus on leverage and we scale our compute to scale our impact.", "approx_timestamp": "0:23" },
    { "text": "Without the agent harness, there are no agents, no agentic coding, and that means there is no agentic engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "0:57" },
    { "text": "The Claude code leak tells us that the agent harness is the product.", "approx_timestamp": "1:38" },
    { "text": "One of the most viable skills an agentic engineer can learn is harness engineering.", "approx_timestamp": "1:50" },
    { "text": "When you stop vibe coding and you start agentic engineering teams of agents in your agent harness, you can solve problem classes, not just one-off tasks.", "approx_timestamp": "1:55" },
    { "text": "One agent is not enough... what we really want here is teams of agents that remember and teams of agents that can execute like you can. You observe, you act, you learn, and then you iterate.", "approx_timestamp": "5:23" },
    { "text": "We need to make sure that our input to the system doesn't scale with the number of agents that we have.", "approx_timestamp": "5:54" },
    { "text": "We now have a not a to-do list, not a to-done list, we have a till-done list. So, our agents are going to work until all these tasks are complete.", "approx_timestamp": "6:33" },
    { "text": "Our orchestrator and our leads don't do any work. They're thinkers, they're managers, they're leaders, most importantly, they're delegators.", "approx_timestamp": "6:49" },
    { "text": "I'm using Cloud Code as a meta builder, a meta agent. When I'm in Cloud Code usually I'm building the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "8:20" },
    { "text": "There is very little value in prompting your agent to build the thing. What you want to be doing instead is... build a team of agents that knows how to build the application on your behalf.", "approx_timestamp": "8:35" },
    { "text": "This team operates this product.", "approx_timestamp": "11:01" },
    { "text": "The workers aren't working, so I have to do this myself. Very team lead-like.", "approx_timestamp": "13:44" },
    { "text": "The agent operates, controls, and tracks whatever it thinks it needs to. I don't touch this file ever.", "approx_timestamp": "16:28" },
    { "text": "The front matter is where a lot of the magic happens.", "approx_timestamp": "18:16" },
    { "text": "We are hot loading the skills into the system prompt, making our agent adhere to them more strongly.", "approx_timestamp": "18:20" },
    { "text": "Specialization and that focused context window, one agent, one prompt, one purpose, is a massive advantage in these multi-agent team systems.", "approx_timestamp": "18:51" },
    { "text": "What I'm doing here is gaining full control over the core four context model prompt and tools. And to gain maximum control, you really need control of the agent harness.", "approx_timestamp": "20:02" },
    { "text": "Delegate is literally a tool. We're using information-dense keywords inside of our workflows to communicate maximum information.", "approx_timestamp": "21:46" },
    { "text": "Like 80% of engineering work and of knowledge work, frankly, probably 90% is a workflow. It's a series of tasks.", "approx_timestamp": "22:06" },
    { "text": "At scale, one prompt is not enough. I said that years ago, I was right.", "approx_timestamp": "24:56" },
    { "text": "Owning the agent harness and having the ability to build out your specialized solution for your specialized problem is one of the highest leverage things any engineer can do right now.", "approx_timestamp": "25:48" },
    { "text": "Big themes to focus on: harness engineering, multi-agent orchestration, and then trust and scale.", "approx_timestamp": "26:03" },
    { "text": "Coding by hand is absolutely dead. You want to start templating. You want to template your engineering into your agent system prompts, into skills, into reusable prompts.", "approx_timestamp": "27:32" },
    { "text": "The theme of 2026 is increasing the trust you have in your agents to do larger scales of work over time.", "approx_timestamp": "31:56" }

    "Three tiers: orchestrator and leads think, plan, and delegate (they don't write files); workers do. Enforce it structurally with per-agent tools + domain, not just prose.",
    "Your input must not scale with agent count. One orchestrator interface; horizontal team scaling behind it.",
    "Owning the harness means owning the core four per agent: context (shared + expertise), model (per-agent, swappable), prompt (system + reusable workflow), tools (delegate/tilldone vs write/edit vs read-only) — plus domain path-scoping.",
    "Front matter is the specialization surface: expertise (mental model), skills (hot-loaded behavior), tools, domain. One agent, one prompt, one purpose.",
    "Agents that keep persistent mental models compound across sessions — but they start empty and grow at runtime; the human doesn't hand-write them.",

    "Claude Code stays in the loop as the meta-agent that builds the system that builds the system — in ands, not ors.",
    "The goal is trust at scale: increase, over time, how much work you trust your agents to do — until they operate your product end to end."

input.content:
# Infinite UI Agents — Master Teaching Notes

**Lesson:** `ma-3-ui-agents` · MA / Agentic Horizon (asset 3 of the trilogy) · order 17 · 32:26 · YouTube `RairMJflUSA` (uploaded 2026-04-06)
**Tactic:** **Own the Harness (Harness Engineering)** — stop solving one-off tasks with a single agent; own the agent harness and engineer specialized teams of learning agents inside it, so you operate whole problem classes.
**Codebase:** `agentic-horizon-extras/ui-agents` (member asset, single commit `7d36778`).

This lesson is a **live showcase**, not a step-by-step build like TAC-1. Dan runs a multi-team agent system on camera (and it partially fails on purpose-revealing ways), then tours the harness that produced it. The teaching job is to extract the durable ideas from a fast, dense demo and to be honest about the gap between **what Dan shows on screen** and **what ships in the committed asset** (see the Accuracy Ledger at the end).

Teaching frame for every idea below: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name (Dan's term) → Failure mode → Retrieval.**

---

## The one-sentence spine

> The Claude Code source-code leak told the whole industry one thing worth acting on: **the agent harness is the product.** Models are commoditizing; the durable leverage is the harness around them — and the skill that captures it is *harness engineering*. When you stop prompting one agent to build one thing and instead own a harness that runs **teams of specialized, learning agents**, you solve entire problem classes — like generating infinite, brand-consistent UI — with a single command to a single orchestrator.

Everything else is detail on that sentence.

---

## Idea 1 — The agent harness is the product

**Hook.** Claude Code leaks. Every tech channel races to cover the features and the new "Mythos model." Dan asks a different question: *what is the $2.5B ARR actually built on?* Not the model — the harness.

**Picture.** Dan's six-part definition of the harness (render as a diagram — it's a talking-head title card in the video): **deterministic code · token caching · agent orchestration · prompts · skills · model control.** (frame beat: `harness-six-components`, diagram.)

**Worked example.** In this very repo the "harness" is legible in one tiny file, `.pi/settings.json`:
```json
{ "thinking": "high", "autoCompact": true, "compactThreshold": 0.8, "prompts": ["./prompts/multi-team"] }
```
That's thinking budget + context auto-compaction (at 80%) + registration of the reusable prompt directory. The rest of the harness surface — which model, which tools, which files each agent may touch — lives per agent in front matter. Owning those knobs is "owning the harness."

**Name.** "**The agent harness is the product.**" And the load-bearing claim: *"Without the agent harness, there are no agents, no agentic coding, and that means there is no agentic engineering."* (0:57)

**Failure mode.** Treating the lesson as a hot-take on the leak (features, drama, the Mythos model). The signal is structural, not gossip: models commoditize, so invest one level down.

**Retrieval.** *What did the Claude Code leak signal, and why does it make harness engineering — not model choice — the skill to invest in?*

---

## Idea 2 — Harness engineering: solve problem classes, not one-off tasks

**Hook.** You could sit in a single Claude Code / Codex / open-code instance and build one UI. Dan did *not* do that. He built a system that builds infinite UIs.

**Picture.** The README tagline, on screen at 16:10 (frame `harness-filetree-readme`): *"Stop solving one off tasks with agents. Build systems (agent teams) that solve entire problem classes."*

**Worked example.** The problem class here is "brand-consistent UI generation." Instead of prompting for a landing page, Dan built four specialized teams (Setup, Brand, UI Generation, Validation) that already understand the domain, then drives them with one command: `/generate aegis app agent-stream 3 "<brief>"`. One sentence → three validated, brand-faithful Vue components on disk. Because **80–90% of engineering (and knowledge) work is a workflow — a series of tasks** — you systematize the workflow once and rerun it forever.

**Name.** "**Harness engineering**" / *"solve problem classes, not just one-off tasks"* (1:55). And the sharp version: *"There is very little value in prompting your agent to build the thing. What you want to be doing instead is... build a team of agents that knows how to build the application on your behalf."* (8:35)

**Failure mode.** Hearing "own the harness" as "abandon Claude Code." Dan is emphatic — *"in ands not ors."* He spends ~80% of his time in Claude Code, but as the **meta-agent** building the systems that then run the product. (See Idea 9.)

**Retrieval.** *Why is prompting an agent to "build the thing" low-value, and what do you build instead?*

---

## Idea 3 — Three tiers: orchestrator → leads → workers (and leads don't write files)

**Hook.** In a great engineering org, leads don't type the code — they plan, delegate, and unblock. Dan builds that org out of agents.

**Picture.** The Pi terminal prints the team as an indented tree (frame `agent-teams-hierarchy-models`, 5:52):
```
Orchestrator (claude-sonnet-4-6)
├─ Setup Lead → Scaffold Worker, Structure Validator
├─ Brand Lead → Brand Analyst
├─ UI Generation Lead → Vue Generator, Animation Specialist   (×A/B/C)
└─ Validation Lead → Soft Validator, Hard Validator           (×A/B/C)
```

**Worked example.** The rule lives in `CLAUDE.md` and is **enforced structurally**, not just requested:
- Leads/orchestrator front matter grants `delegate` + `tilldone` tools, but their `domain:` permissions set `upsert: false` on `apps/infinite-ui/` — they *cannot* write product files, only their own mental model.
- Workers (Vue Generator, Scaffold Worker, Animation Specialist, Brand Analyst) grant `write`/`edit`/`bash` and carry the `precise-worker` skill ("Execute exactly what your lead assigned — no improvising").
- Read-only validators (Soft/Hard/Structure) have *no* write/edit tool at all — they report PASS/FAIL, they never fix.

**Name.** *"Our orchestrator and our leads don't do any work. They're thinkers, they're managers, they're leaders, most importantly, they're delegators."* (6:49) The committed shape: **1 orchestrator + 8 teams = 24 agent slots, backed by 12 unique agent files.**

**Failure mode.** Thinking leads are idle because "they don't work." Their job is classify → delegate → synthesize; removing the write-block turns leads into workers and collapses the tiering (which is exactly what you'll watch happen under stress in Idea 7).

**Retrieval.** *Who writes files and who doesn't in the three tiers — and what two front-matter fields enforce it?*

---

## Idea 4 — One orchestrator interface: your input must not scale with agent count

**Hook.** Add ten agents and, naively, you now have ten things to prompt and babysit. That's a trap — you just became the bottleneck.

**Picture.** The chat layout Dan narrates (5:40–6:47): "scale on the left, structure and communication on the right, chat system on top." You type once, to one orchestrator; the fan-out is invisible to you.

**Worked example.** `orchestrator.md` classifies the request, opens a `tilldone` list, and delegates via the `delegate(team, question)` tool. When Dan wants three new UIs he pastes **one** reusable prompt; the orchestrator @-mentions the Setup team with a full engineered prompt of its own. Dan's phrase: *"I have taught my orchestrator how to prompt engineer."* Horizontal team scaling behind a constant-size human interface.

**Name.** *"We need to make sure that our input to the system doesn't scale with the number of agents that we have."* (5:54)

**Failure mode.** Bolting on more agents/teams while also opening more chats to steer them — reintroducing yourself as the scaling bottleneck the architecture exists to remove.

**Retrieval.** *Why is "one orchestrator interface" a hard requirement rather than a convenience?*

---

## Idea 5 — Front-matter specialization: own the core four per agent

**Hook.** What actually makes a "front-end-only" or "billing-only" agent real, instead of a system prompt that says "please only touch the front end"?

**Picture.** The Vue Generator's front matter, fully legible on screen (frame `agent-frontmatter-specialization`, 17:58):
```yaml
name: vue-generator
model: stepfun/step-3.5-flash        # per-agent model — swappable
expertise:                            # its persistent mental model
  - path: .pi/multi-team/expertise/vue-generator-mental-model.yaml
    updatable: true
    max-lines: 10000
skills:                               # hot-loaded behavior
  - mental-model / active-listener / precise-worker / parallel-mental-model-updates
tools: [read, write, edit, bash, grep, find, ls]
domain:                               # the exact paths it may act on
  - path: apps/infinite-ui/           # read + upsert, no delete
```

**Worked example.** This is the **core four (context, model, prompt, tools)**, set independently for one agent:
- **context** = shared_context files + this agent's expertise file + its session log;
- **model** = `stepfun/step-3.5-flash` here (committed default is `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`);
- **prompt** = the system-prompt body with `{{EXPERTISE_BLOCK}}` / `{{SKILLS_BLOCK}}` injected;
- **tools** = `write/edit/bash` (a doer), no `delegate`;
- plus **`domain`** — the sleeper control — path-scopes where those tools may operate. Dan: *"you can specialize agents to just run on your front end, to just run on your back end, ... your database migrations, ... your devops, ... your billing."*

**Name.** *"The front matter is where a lot of the magic happens."* (18:16) *"We are hot loading the skills into the system prompt."* (18:20) *"One agent, one prompt, one purpose."* (18:51 — Dan's verbal framing; the `precise-worker` skill encodes it in the repo.) *"Full control over the core four ... you really need control of the agent harness."* (20:02)

**Failure mode.** Reading specialization as "just a good system prompt." It's four coordinated controls; skip `domain` and your "focused" agent can still wander the whole repo.

**Retrieval.** *Name the four front-matter fields that specialize an agent, and say which one makes "front-end-only" scoping actually real.*

---

## Idea 6 — Agents that learn: persistent mental models

**Hook.** Spinning up parallel agents with blank memories is an improvement. Teams of agents that *remember* — that observe, act, learn, and iterate like you do — is the real prize.

**Picture.** `vue-generator-mental-model.yaml` open in VS Code (frame `mental-model-7k-tokens`, 16:55): dated `2026-04-02`, full of self-authored patterns — `glassmorphism_split_panel`, `spacing_pattern: "calc(var(--space-unit) * N)"`, `glow_pattern`, `sfc_rules`, `breakpoints` — with **`Tokens: 7753`** in the status bar.

**Worked example.** Each agent owns a YAML expertise file. A ~77-line skill, `mental-model.md`, teaches it the loop: **read at task start; after meaningful work, update (rewrite stale entries, don't just append); after every write, `wc -l` and trim to `max-lines`, then validate the YAML parses.** Dan: *"I don't touch this file ever. All I've done here is give this agent a skill, which very, very simply tells it how to manage its mental model."* (16:28) In parallel A/B/C teams, sibling instances share one file — the `parallel-mental-model-updates` skill reframes write-conflicts as "coordination signals, not bugs."

**Name.** "**Agents that learn / mental models**." *"Teams of agents that remember... You observe, you act, you learn, and then you iterate."* (5:23)

**Failure mode (critical accuracy point).** Believing the mental models ship pre-filled. **In the committed repo all 12 expertise files are one-line stubs** (`# Mental model — auto-maintained by agent`). The 7,753-token file Dan shows is **runtime state** he accumulated. Clone the asset and you start empty; the agents grow their own knowledge as you run them.

**Retrieval.** *How does an agent "learn" here — and what will you actually find in `expertise/*.yaml` the moment you clone the repo?*

---

## Idea 7 — Model control and reliability: heterogeneous models, graceful failure

**Hook.** Owning the harness means you can put a different model behind every agent — and swap it the instant it misbehaves. Dan proves it by *letting it misbehave on camera.*

**Picture.** Two beats:
1. The team tree shows the model per line: Vue Generator = `stepfun/step-3.5-flash`, Vue Generator (B) = `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7`, everyone else `claude-sonnet-4-6` (frame `agent-teams-hierarchy-models`).
2. The lead breaks the rule (frame `lead-writes-when-worker-fails`, 13:26): *"Vue Generator (B) is not writing to disk. Given the silent failure, I need to write the complete SFC myself. As a lead, I normally delegate — but my only team member is non-functional. The CLAUDE.md rules say workers write files, but with a broken worker, I need to produce the output directly to fulfill the task."*

**Worked example.** Teams A and B (open-source models) return "no response"; team C (Sonnet) works. The leads (Claude) detect the dead workers and finish the components themselves — very team-lead-like. Nothing stalls; the pipeline still delivers 3 validated variants. Dan: *"I could easily add a model rotation system into this... if this model is not working, swap it out."* The README's *"Recommended: Use Claude series models... proven reliable"* is the same lesson stated calmly.

**Name.** "**Model control / reliability & redundancy.**" *"At scale, one prompt is not enough."* (24:56)

**Failure mode.** Reading the demo's failures as the *idea* failing. The failures are the argument: because Dan owns the harness, a broken model is survivable — redundancy and rotation keep results flowing. (And: assuming the whole repo runs open-source models — on disk every agent is Sonnet; the open-source swaps were live, uncommitted edits.)

**Retrieval.** *The open-source teams failed mid-demo. Give two reasons that's evidence FOR the tactic.*

---

## Idea 8 — Reusable prompts against teams, the till-done list, and "delegate" as a tool

**Hook.** Once you own a team, you can write prompts *for the team* — a command that drives an entire workflow top to bottom.

**Picture.** The `/generate` command and the TillDone list. The 8-step pipeline in `generate.md`; the running list on screen: `TillDone: Aegis Agent Stream Generation [1/8] ... [11/11]` (frames `parallel-teams-tilldone`, `orchestrator-final-report`).

**Worked example.** `/generate <brand> <product> <tree> <count> <brief>` — consistent **Variables / Instructions / Workflow / Report** shape — runs: (1) Setup scaffolds + writes `trees.yaml`/`activity.yaml` + Zod-validates → (2) Brand loads `brand.yaml` → (3) UI Gen Lead writes N differentiated briefs → (4) **round-robin** branch 1→UI Gen, 2→UI Gen B, 3→UI Gen C, generate in parallel → (5) Setup flips `generating→validating` → (6) round-robin validate across Validation A/B/C → (7) route failures back to the generating team → (8) Setup flips to `validated/failed`, clears `activity.yaml`. The routing vocabulary is deliberately terse: *"Delegate is literally a tool. We're using information-dense keywords... to communicate maximum information."* (21:46)

**Name.** "**Reusable prompts / workflow commands**" and the "**till-done list**" — *"not a to-do list, not a to-done list, we have a till-done list... our agents are going to work until all these tasks are complete."* (6:33)

**Failure mode.** Treating `/generate` as "just a prompt." It's an 8-step, multi-team, round-robin, validated pipeline. *Accuracy nuance:* the committed `generate.md` intentionally carries **no** till-done list (per `specs/parallel-team-duplication.md`, a coordination stress-test); the on-screen TillDone is the orchestrator's own `tilldone` tool. Both are true.

**Retrieval.** *What does `/generate` take, roughly what are its stages, and where does the on-screen "till-done" list actually come from?*

---

## Idea 9 — Claude Code as meta-agent, and the theme of 2026: trust and scale

**Hook.** If the specialized Pi harness runs the product, what runs the *building* of that harness? Claude Code.

**Picture.** Dan's two-tool split, stated repeatedly: *"80% of the time I'm spinning up Cloud Code agents to not work on the actual product... I'm using Cloud Code as a meta builder, a meta agent... building the system that builds the system."* (8:20)

**Worked example.** In this repo, `.claude/commands/` (build, install, plan-w-team, prime) and `.claude/skills/` (bowser = playwright-cli, drive = tmux automation, svg-generate, tts-eleven) are the Claude-Code meta-layer that scaffolds, primes, validates, and drives the Pi multi-team system. `plan-w-team.md` even documents Claude Code's own TaskCreate/addBlockedBy team API — Claude Code builds and orchestrates the thing that then operates the product.

**Name.** "**Claude Code as meta agent**" and the closing thesis: *"The theme of 2026 is increasing the trust you have in your agents to do larger scales of work over time."* (31:56) The two skills to invest in: **harness engineering + multi-agent orchestration**, both underlined by **trust and scale** (26:03).

**Failure mode.** Chasing scale for its own sake. Scale without trust is noise; you build closed, specialized systems precisely so you can trust them with more work.

**Retrieval.** *What does Dan use Claude Code for ~80% of the time, and what single theme does he say underlines both harness engineering and multi-agent orchestration?*

---

## The Infinite UI system (the demo, mapped to the repo)

- **What it builds:** infinite brand-consistent Vue UI. Define brand identity once (`brand.yaml`), generate unlimited variants, browse them all in one Vue app.
- **Hierarchy:** **Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf.** `aegis` → `app`/`mobile`/`site` → `agent-stream`/`dashboard`/... → `v1`/`v2`/`v3` → `index.vue`. On disk: **1 real brand, 3 products, 7 trees, 23 real generated leaves** (+2 template stubs). The demo's `agent-stream` tree holds exactly the three UIs Dan browses: `compact-dashboard`, `glassmorphism-panel` (972 lines), `timeline-stack` (899 lines — matches his on-screen "899-line SFC").
- **Zero hardcoded values:** every leaf uses CSS custom properties from `brand.yaml`; edit a token → live rebrand.
- **Live preview (accuracy):** a validated branch renders as a real `<iframe>` (1280×720, CSS-scaled, `pointer-events:none`) into the leaf's gallery route, which uses `import.meta.glob` + dynamic `<component :is>`. Dan guesses "teleport"; Vue's Teleport is used only in `Sidebar.vue`.
- **Stack:** Vue 3.5 / Vite 8 / Pinia 3 / vue-router 5 / TS 5.9 / Bun; `@vue-flow/core` + `@dagrejs/dagre` (canvas); `zod` + `yaml` (validated manifests).
- **The four teams:** Setup (scaffold + trees.yaml + Zod), Brand (guard identity, briefs, contrast), UI Generation (write Vue SFCs), Validation (Playwright screenshots, brand/responsive/a11y). Tripled to A/B/C for UI Gen + Validation.

---

## VTT-verified timeline map

| 0:00–2:10 | Claude Code leak → "the harness is the product"; harness engineering is the skill | diagram: six harness components |

| 26:25–32:26 | Agentic Horizon pitch; solve problem classes not tasks; Claude Code as meta-agent; theme of 2026 = trust at scale | — |

---

## Glossary (canonical terms + transcript mishearings)

- **Agent harness** — everything around the model that makes agents possible: deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, model control. "The product."
- **Harness engineering** — building/specializing your own agent harness for your domain (Dan uses the Pi coding agent).
- **Pi coding agent** — the granular-control agent tool at pi.dev. *(Transcript: "pie coding agent" / "PyCoding agent." Title confirms "Pi.")*
- **Core four** — context, model, prompt, tools; owned per-agent via front matter when you control the harness.
- **Orchestrator / lead / worker / validator** — the four roles. Orchestrator + leads delegate (never write files); workers write; validators are read-only reporters.
- **`delegate` / `tilldone`** — literal tools. `delegate(team, question)` routes to a team lead; `tilldone` manages the "work-until-complete" task list.
- **Till-done list** — a task list agents work until every item is done. *(Intentional wordplay, not a mishearing.)*
- **Expertise file / mental model** — a per-agent YAML the agent self-maintains (`.pi/multi-team/expertise/*.yaml`); empty stub in the committed repo, grows at runtime to `max-lines: 10000`.
- **`domain` (front matter)** — path-scoped read/upsert/delete permissions; makes "front-end-only" agents real.
- **Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf** — the Infinite UI hierarchy; a Leaf is the generated `index.vue`.
- **Aegis** — the demo brand, an "agent security command center." *(Transcript: "Egis.")*
- **Agentix / Indydevdan** — the other two on-screen brands (not committed). *(Transcript: "AgentX / AgentDan.")*
- **Round-robin** — orchestrator assigns branch 1→A, 2→B, 3→C, 4→A... across the parallel teams.
- **Mythos model** — a real model name referenced re: the Claude Code leak (per the official description), not a mishearing.
- **Claude Code as meta-agent** — using Claude Code (~80% of the time) to build the system that runs the product. *(Transcript: "Cloud Code.")*
- **Model IDs seen on screen** — `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` (committed default), `stepfun/step-3.5-flash`, `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7`. *(Transcript: "Sonic," "step 3.5 flash," "minimax 2.7.")*
