# Infinite UI Agents — Master Teaching Notes

**Lesson:** `ma-3-ui-agents` · MA / Agentic Horizon (asset 3 of the trilogy) · order 17 · 32:26 · YouTube `RairMJflUSA` (uploaded 2026-04-06)
**Tactic:** **Own the Harness (Harness Engineering)** — stop solving one-off tasks with a single agent; own the agent harness and engineer specialized teams of learning agents inside it, so you operate whole problem classes.
**Codebase:** `agentic-horizon-extras/ui-agents` (member asset, single commit `7d36778`).

This lesson is a **live showcase**, not a step-by-step build like TAC-1. Dan runs a multi-team agent system on camera (and it partially fails on purpose-revealing ways), then tours the harness that produced it. The teaching job is to extract the durable ideas from a fast, dense demo and to be honest about the gap between **what Dan shows on screen** and **what ships in the committed asset** (see the Accuracy Ledger at the end).

Teaching frame for every idea below: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name (Dan's term) → Failure mode → Retrieval.**

---

## The one-sentence spine

> The Claude Code source-code leak told the whole industry one thing worth acting on: **the agent harness is the product.** Models are commoditizing; the durable leverage is the harness around them — and the skill that captures it is *harness engineering*. When you stop prompting one agent to build one thing and instead own a harness that runs **teams of specialized, learning agents**, you solve entire problem classes — like generating infinite, brand-consistent UI — with a single command to a single orchestrator.

Everything else is detail on that sentence.

---

## Idea 1 — The agent harness is the product

**Hook.** Claude Code leaks. Every tech channel races to cover the features and the new "Mythos model." Dan asks a different question: *what is the $2.5B ARR actually built on?* Not the model — the harness.

**Picture.** Dan's six-part definition of the harness (render as a diagram — it's a talking-head title card in the video): **deterministic code · token caching · agent orchestration · prompts · skills · model control.** (frame beat: `harness-six-components`, diagram.)

**Worked example.** In this very repo the "harness" is legible in one tiny file, `.pi/settings.json`:
```json
{ "thinking": "high", "autoCompact": true, "compactThreshold": 0.8, "prompts": ["./prompts/multi-team"] }
```
That's thinking budget + context auto-compaction (at 80%) + registration of the reusable prompt directory. The rest of the harness surface — which model, which tools, which files each agent may touch — lives per agent in front matter. Owning those knobs is "owning the harness."

**Name.** "**The agent harness is the product.**" And the load-bearing claim: *"Without the agent harness, there are no agents, no agentic coding, and that means there is no agentic engineering."* (0:57)

**Failure mode.** Treating the lesson as a hot-take on the leak (features, drama, the Mythos model). The signal is structural, not gossip: models commoditize, so invest one level down.

**Retrieval.** *What did the Claude Code leak signal, and why does it make harness engineering — not model choice — the skill to invest in?*

---

## Idea 2 — Harness engineering: solve problem classes, not one-off tasks

**Hook.** You could sit in a single Claude Code / Codex / open-code instance and build one UI. Dan did *not* do that. He built a system that builds infinite UIs.

**Picture.** The README tagline, on screen at 16:10 (frame `harness-filetree-readme`): *"Stop solving one off tasks with agents. Build systems (agent teams) that solve entire problem classes."*

**Worked example.** The problem class here is "brand-consistent UI generation." Instead of prompting for a landing page, Dan built four specialized teams (Setup, Brand, UI Generation, Validation) that already understand the domain, then drives them with one command: `/generate aegis app agent-stream 3 "<brief>"`. One sentence → three validated, brand-faithful Vue components on disk. Because **80–90% of engineering (and knowledge) work is a workflow — a series of tasks** — you systematize the workflow once and rerun it forever.

**Name.** "**Harness engineering**" / *"solve problem classes, not just one-off tasks"* (1:55). And the sharp version: *"There is very little value in prompting your agent to build the thing. What you want to be doing instead is... build a team of agents that knows how to build the application on your behalf."* (8:35)

**Failure mode.** Hearing "own the harness" as "abandon Claude Code." Dan is emphatic — *"in ands not ors."* He spends ~80% of his time in Claude Code, but as the **meta-agent** building the systems that then run the product. (See Idea 9.)

**Retrieval.** *Why is prompting an agent to "build the thing" low-value, and what do you build instead?*

---

## Idea 3 — Three tiers: orchestrator → leads → workers (and leads don't write files)

**Hook.** In a great engineering org, leads don't type the code — they plan, delegate, and unblock. Dan builds that org out of agents.

**Picture.** The Pi terminal prints the team as an indented tree (frame `agent-teams-hierarchy-models`, 5:52):
```
Orchestrator (claude-sonnet-4-6)
├─ Setup Lead → Scaffold Worker, Structure Validator
├─ Brand Lead → Brand Analyst
├─ UI Generation Lead → Vue Generator, Animation Specialist   (×A/B/C)
└─ Validation Lead → Soft Validator, Hard Validator           (×A/B/C)
```

**Worked example.** The rule lives in `CLAUDE.md` and is **enforced structurally**, not just requested:
- Leads/orchestrator front matter grants `delegate` + `tilldone` tools, but their `domain:` permissions set `upsert: false` on `apps/infinite-ui/` — they *cannot* write product files, only their own mental model.
- Workers (Vue Generator, Scaffold Worker, Animation Specialist, Brand Analyst) grant `write`/`edit`/`bash` and carry the `precise-worker` skill ("Execute exactly what your lead assigned — no improvising").
- Read-only validators (Soft/Hard/Structure) have *no* write/edit tool at all — they report PASS/FAIL, they never fix.

**Name.** *"Our orchestrator and our leads don't do any work. They're thinkers, they're managers, they're leaders, most importantly, they're delegators."* (6:49) The committed shape: **1 orchestrator + 8 teams = 24 agent slots, backed by 12 unique agent files.**

**Failure mode.** Thinking leads are idle because "they don't work." Their job is classify → delegate → synthesize; removing the write-block turns leads into workers and collapses the tiering (which is exactly what you'll watch happen under stress in Idea 7).

**Retrieval.** *Who writes files and who doesn't in the three tiers — and what two front-matter fields enforce it?*

---

## Idea 4 — One orchestrator interface: your input must not scale with agent count

**Hook.** Add ten agents and, naively, you now have ten things to prompt and babysit. That's a trap — you just became the bottleneck.

**Picture.** The chat layout Dan narrates (5:40–6:47): "scale on the left, structure and communication on the right, chat system on top." You type once, to one orchestrator; the fan-out is invisible to you.

**Worked example.** `orchestrator.md` classifies the request, opens a `tilldone` list, and delegates via the `delegate(team, question)` tool. When Dan wants three new UIs he pastes **one** reusable prompt; the orchestrator @-mentions the Setup team with a full engineered prompt of its own. Dan's phrase: *"I have taught my orchestrator how to prompt engineer."* Horizontal team scaling behind a constant-size human interface.

**Name.** *"We need to make sure that our input to the system doesn't scale with the number of agents that we have."* (5:54)

**Failure mode.** Bolting on more agents/teams while also opening more chats to steer them — reintroducing yourself as the scaling bottleneck the architecture exists to remove.

**Retrieval.** *Why is "one orchestrator interface" a hard requirement rather than a convenience?*

---

## Idea 5 — Front-matter specialization: own the core four per agent

**Hook.** What actually makes a "front-end-only" or "billing-only" agent real, instead of a system prompt that says "please only touch the front end"?

**Picture.** The Vue Generator's front matter, fully legible on screen (frame `agent-frontmatter-specialization`, 17:58):
```yaml
name: vue-generator
model: stepfun/step-3.5-flash        # per-agent model — swappable
expertise:                            # its persistent mental model
  - path: .pi/multi-team/expertise/vue-generator-mental-model.yaml
    updatable: true
    max-lines: 10000
skills:                               # hot-loaded behavior
  - mental-model / active-listener / precise-worker / parallel-mental-model-updates
tools: [read, write, edit, bash, grep, find, ls]
domain:                               # the exact paths it may act on
  - path: apps/infinite-ui/           # read + upsert, no delete
```

**Worked example.** This is the **core four (context, model, prompt, tools)**, set independently for one agent:
- **context** = shared_context files + this agent's expertise file + its session log;
- **model** = `stepfun/step-3.5-flash` here (committed default is `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`);
- **prompt** = the system-prompt body with `{{EXPERTISE_BLOCK}}` / `{{SKILLS_BLOCK}}` injected;
- **tools** = `write/edit/bash` (a doer), no `delegate`;
- plus **`domain`** — the sleeper control — path-scopes where those tools may operate. Dan: *"you can specialize agents to just run on your front end, to just run on your back end, ... your database migrations, ... your devops, ... your billing."*

**Name.** *"The front matter is where a lot of the magic happens."* (18:16) *"We are hot loading the skills into the system prompt."* (18:20) *"One agent, one prompt, one purpose."* (18:51 — Dan's verbal framing; the `precise-worker` skill encodes it in the repo.) *"Full control over the core four ... you really need control of the agent harness."* (20:02)

**Failure mode.** Reading specialization as "just a good system prompt." It's four coordinated controls; skip `domain` and your "focused" agent can still wander the whole repo.

**Retrieval.** *Name the four front-matter fields that specialize an agent, and say which one makes "front-end-only" scoping actually real.*

---

## Idea 6 — Agents that learn: persistent mental models

**Hook.** Spinning up parallel agents with blank memories is an improvement. Teams of agents that *remember* — that observe, act, learn, and iterate like you do — is the real prize.

**Picture.** `vue-generator-mental-model.yaml` open in VS Code (frame `mental-model-7k-tokens`, 16:55): dated `2026-04-02`, full of self-authored patterns — `glassmorphism_split_panel`, `spacing_pattern: "calc(var(--space-unit) * N)"`, `glow_pattern`, `sfc_rules`, `breakpoints` — with **`Tokens: 7753`** in the status bar.

**Worked example.** Each agent owns a YAML expertise file. A ~77-line skill, `mental-model.md`, teaches it the loop: **read at task start; after meaningful work, update (rewrite stale entries, don't just append); after every write, `wc -l` and trim to `max-lines`, then validate the YAML parses.** Dan: *"I don't touch this file ever. All I've done here is give this agent a skill, which very, very simply tells it how to manage its mental model."* (16:28) In parallel A/B/C teams, sibling instances share one file — the `parallel-mental-model-updates` skill reframes write-conflicts as "coordination signals, not bugs."

**Name.** "**Agents that learn / mental models**." *"Teams of agents that remember... You observe, you act, you learn, and then you iterate."* (5:23)

**Failure mode (critical accuracy point).** Believing the mental models ship pre-filled. **In the committed repo all 12 expertise files are one-line stubs** (`# Mental model — auto-maintained by agent`). The 7,753-token file Dan shows is **runtime state** he accumulated. Clone the asset and you start empty; the agents grow their own knowledge as you run them.

**Retrieval.** *How does an agent "learn" here — and what will you actually find in `expertise/*.yaml` the moment you clone the repo?*

---

## Idea 7 — Model control and reliability: heterogeneous models, graceful failure

**Hook.** Owning the harness means you can put a different model behind every agent — and swap it the instant it misbehaves. Dan proves it by *letting it misbehave on camera.*

**Picture.** Two beats:
1. The team tree shows the model per line: Vue Generator = `stepfun/step-3.5-flash`, Vue Generator (B) = `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7`, everyone else `claude-sonnet-4-6` (frame `agent-teams-hierarchy-models`).
2. The lead breaks the rule (frame `lead-writes-when-worker-fails`, 13:26): *"Vue Generator (B) is not writing to disk. Given the silent failure, I need to write the complete SFC myself. As a lead, I normally delegate — but my only team member is non-functional. The CLAUDE.md rules say workers write files, but with a broken worker, I need to produce the output directly to fulfill the task."*

**Worked example.** Teams A and B (open-source models) return "no response"; team C (Sonnet) works. The leads (Claude) detect the dead workers and finish the components themselves — very team-lead-like. Nothing stalls; the pipeline still delivers 3 validated variants. Dan: *"I could easily add a model rotation system into this... if this model is not working, swap it out."* The README's *"Recommended: Use Claude series models... proven reliable"* is the same lesson stated calmly.

**Name.** "**Model control / reliability & redundancy.**" *"At scale, one prompt is not enough."* (24:56)

**Failure mode.** Reading the demo's failures as the *idea* failing. The failures are the argument: because Dan owns the harness, a broken model is survivable — redundancy and rotation keep results flowing. (And: assuming the whole repo runs open-source models — on disk every agent is Sonnet; the open-source swaps were live, uncommitted edits.)

**Retrieval.** *The open-source teams failed mid-demo. Give two reasons that's evidence FOR the tactic.*

---

## Idea 8 — Reusable prompts against teams, the till-done list, and "delegate" as a tool

**Hook.** Once you own a team, you can write prompts *for the team* — a command that drives an entire workflow top to bottom.

**Picture.** The `/generate` command and the TillDone list. The 8-step pipeline in `generate.md`; the running list on screen: `TillDone: Aegis Agent Stream Generation [1/8] ... [11/11]` (frames `parallel-teams-tilldone`, `orchestrator-final-report`).

**Worked example.** `/generate <brand> <product> <tree> <count> <brief>` — consistent **Variables / Instructions / Workflow / Report** shape — runs: (1) Setup scaffolds + writes `trees.yaml`/`activity.yaml` + Zod-validates → (2) Brand loads `brand.yaml` → (3) UI Gen Lead writes N differentiated briefs → (4) **round-robin** branch 1→UI Gen, 2→UI Gen B, 3→UI Gen C, generate in parallel → (5) Setup flips `generating→validating` → (6) round-robin validate across Validation A/B/C → (7) route failures back to the generating team → (8) Setup flips to `validated/failed`, clears `activity.yaml`. The routing vocabulary is deliberately terse: *"Delegate is literally a tool. We're using information-dense keywords... to communicate maximum information."* (21:46)

**Name.** "**Reusable prompts / workflow commands**" and the "**till-done list**" — *"not a to-do list, not a to-done list, we have a till-done list... our agents are going to work until all these tasks are complete."* (6:33)

**Failure mode.** Treating `/generate` as "just a prompt." It's an 8-step, multi-team, round-robin, validated pipeline. *Accuracy nuance:* the committed `generate.md` intentionally carries **no** till-done list (per `specs/parallel-team-duplication.md`, a coordination stress-test); the on-screen TillDone is the orchestrator's own `tilldone` tool. Both are true.

**Retrieval.** *What does `/generate` take, roughly what are its stages, and where does the on-screen "till-done" list actually come from?*

---

## Idea 9 — Claude Code as meta-agent, and the theme of 2026: trust and scale

**Hook.** If the specialized Pi harness runs the product, what runs the *building* of that harness? Claude Code.

**Picture.** Dan's two-tool split, stated repeatedly: *"80% of the time I'm spinning up Cloud Code agents to not work on the actual product... I'm using Cloud Code as a meta builder, a meta agent... building the system that builds the system."* (8:20)

**Worked example.** In this repo, `.claude/commands/` (build, install, plan-w-team, prime) and `.claude/skills/` (bowser = playwright-cli, drive = tmux automation, svg-generate, tts-eleven) are the Claude-Code meta-layer that scaffolds, primes, validates, and drives the Pi multi-team system. `plan-w-team.md` even documents Claude Code's own TaskCreate/addBlockedBy team API — Claude Code builds and orchestrates the thing that then operates the product.

**Name.** "**Claude Code as meta agent**" and the closing thesis: *"The theme of 2026 is increasing the trust you have in your agents to do larger scales of work over time."* (31:56) The two skills to invest in: **harness engineering + multi-agent orchestration**, both underlined by **trust and scale** (26:03).

**Failure mode.** Chasing scale for its own sake. Scale without trust is noise; you build closed, specialized systems precisely so you can trust them with more work.

**Retrieval.** *What does Dan use Claude Code for ~80% of the time, and what single theme does he say underlines both harness engineering and multi-agent orchestration?*

---

## The Infinite UI system (the demo, mapped to the repo)

- **What it builds:** infinite brand-consistent Vue UI. Define brand identity once (`brand.yaml`), generate unlimited variants, browse them all in one Vue app.
- **Hierarchy:** **Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf.** `aegis` → `app`/`mobile`/`site` → `agent-stream`/`dashboard`/... → `v1`/`v2`/`v3` → `index.vue`. On disk: **1 real brand, 3 products, 7 trees, 23 real generated leaves** (+2 template stubs). The demo's `agent-stream` tree holds exactly the three UIs Dan browses: `compact-dashboard`, `glassmorphism-panel` (972 lines), `timeline-stack` (899 lines — matches his on-screen "899-line SFC").
- **Zero hardcoded values:** every leaf uses CSS custom properties from `brand.yaml`; edit a token → live rebrand.
- **Live preview (accuracy):** a validated branch renders as a real `<iframe>` (1280×720, CSS-scaled, `pointer-events:none`) into the leaf's gallery route, which uses `import.meta.glob` + dynamic `<component :is>`. Dan guesses "teleport"; Vue's Teleport is used only in `Sidebar.vue`.
- **Stack:** Vue 3.5 / Vite 8 / Pinia 3 / vue-router 5 / TS 5.9 / Bun; `@vue-flow/core` + `@dagrejs/dagre` (canvas); `zod` + `yaml` (validated manifests).
- **The four teams:** Setup (scaffold + trees.yaml + Zod), Brand (guard identity, briefs, contrast), UI Generation (write Vue SFCs), Validation (Playwright screenshots, brand/responsive/a11y). Tripled to A/B/C for UI Gen + Validation.

input.content:
# Infinite UI Agents — Nuggets for Weak Learners

Sixteen ranked nuggets in three tiers. Tier 1 = the spine you must be able to say out loud. Tier 2 = the mechanics that make it real. Tier 3 = the nuances and honesty flags that separate "watched the video" from "understood the asset." Each nugget: the insight, then **why it matters**.

---

## Tier 1 — The spine (know these cold)

**1. The harness is the product; the model is being commoditized.**
The Claude Code leak's real signal: a $2.5B business is built on the harness (deterministic code, token caching, agent orchestration, prompts, skills, model control), not the model on top.
*Why it matters:* it tells you where to invest — down a level, into the harness — while everyone else argues about model benchmarks.

**2. Stop solving one-off tasks; build teams that solve problem classes.**
Don't prompt an agent to build *the thing*. Build a team of agents that knows how to build (and operate) that whole *class* of things on your behalf.
*Why it matters:* 80–90% of engineering work is a repeatable workflow. Systematize the workflow once; run it forever.

**3. Three tiers: orchestrator → leads → workers. Leads and orchestrator don't write files.**
Orchestrator and leads think, plan, delegate, synthesize. Workers do the writing. Validators only report.
*Why it matters:* it mirrors how great human teams scale — and here it's enforced in code, not just asked for.

**4. Your input must not scale with the number of agents.**
You always talk to one orchestrator, no matter how many agents run behind it. Teams scale horizontally; your interface stays constant.
*Why it matters:* the moment driving the system grows with every added agent, *you* become the bottleneck the whole design exists to remove.

**5. Owning the harness = owning the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) per agent.**
Stock tools give you one blended agent with fixed defaults. The harness lets you set context, model, prompt, and tools independently for every agent.
*Why it matters:* this is the concrete payoff of "own the harness" — otherwise it's a slogan.

**6. The theme of 2026 is trust at scale.**
Harness engineering + multi-agent orchestration are the two skills; trust and scale underline both. Increase, over time, how much work you trust your agents to do — until they run the product end to end.
*Why it matters:* it's the north star that tells you whether you're building the right thing (closed, specialized, trustworthy systems) vs just spawning more agents.

**7. Front matter is the specialization surface: expertise + skills + tools + domain.**
Each agent's YAML front matter sets its mental model (`expertise`), hot-loaded behavior (`skills`), capabilities (`tools`), and — the sleeper — the exact paths it may touch (`domain`).
*Why it matters:* "one agent, one prompt, one purpose" is real only because `domain` path-scopes the agent; without it, "front-end-only" is just a wish.

**8. `delegate` and `tilldone` are literally tools.**
Leads/orchestrator get `delegate(team, question)` and `tilldone`; workers get `write/edit/bash`; validators get neither write nor delegate.
*Why it matters:* the role differences aren't personality — they're the tool list. That's how the "leads don't write" rule is enforced.

**9. Agents keep persistent mental models and grow them across sessions.**

*Why it matters:* this is what "teams that remember" means — each round of work makes the next one better.

**10. `/generate` is an 8-step, multi-team, validated pipeline — not a single prompt.**

# Infinite UI Agents — Outdated vs. Current (course-era → mid-2026)

**Unusual for this lesson:** it is *already* current. Uploaded 2026-04-06, it references the Claude Code source-code leak, Sonnet/Opus 4.6, 1M-context models, Minimax M2.7, Step 3.5 Flash, and "the theme of 2026." So the "outdated" axis here is **not** a stale-tooling problem like TAC-1. It is two different things:

1. **Committed-asset vs. live-demo divergence** — what a reader clones is a snapshot; the video runs a hand-tuned superset. This is the dominant gap, and it's the chapter's chief honesty obligation.
2. **Forward drift** — model IDs and the pace at which the *mainstream* tool (Claude Code) is absorbing harness features.

Each gap below has a **book treatment** the chapter author should apply.

---

## Gap 1 — What ships ≠ what's on screen (the big one)

**Course-era artifact:** the committed member asset `ui-agents` is a single-commit (`7d36778`), all-Claude, empty-mental-model snapshot with one brand. The video runs a superset: `agents-os/` open-source agent variants, `multi-team-config-min.yaml`, mental models populated to ~7,753 tokens, three brands, and open-source models (`stepfun/step-3.5-flash`, `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7`) swapped into specific agents.

**Why it matters:** a reader who clones the asset expecting the demo will think it's broken or incomplete. It isn't — they're starting from the base state.

**Book treatment:** carry the Accuracy Ledger table (in `extract.md`) as a boxed "What you clone vs. what Dan runs" sidebar. Every time the chapter quotes an on-screen model ID, mental-model size, or brand count, add the committed value in adjacent prose. Frame the difference positively: the empty stubs *are* the feature — they grow as you run the system.

---

## Gap 2 — Model IDs are period-specific and will drift fastest

**Course-era artifact:** `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` / `claude-opus-4-6`, `stepfun/step-3.5-flash`, `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7`, the 1M-context Sonnet/Opus, and the "Mythos model" leak reference are all April-2026 specifics.

**Why it matters:** these names age in weeks, not years. A chapter that leans on them reads dated on publish.

**Book treatment:** teach the *durable* claim — **the harness lets you set and rotate the model per agent** — and treat every ID as period detail (label it "as of April 2026"). Keep the reliability lesson (Sonnet proved reliable; open-source teams struggled) as a transferable point about *matching model capability to workload and building in redundancy*, not as a verdict on any specific model. Re-verify all model names at publish.

---

## Gap 3 — The mainstream tool is absorbing the harness

**Course-era framing:** "own the harness with Pi" is sharpest when the mainstream tool (Claude Code) is a black box you can't customize.

**Why it matters:** Claude Code now exposes subagents, hooks, skills, plugins, output styles, permission modes, and settings layering — a large slice of the very harness surface Dan builds in Pi. `plan-w-team.md` in this repo already documents Claude Code's own multi-agent `TaskCreate`/`addBlockedBy` API.

**Book treatment:** don't present it as "Pi vs. Claude Code." Present the *principle* — whoever controls context/model/prompt/tools + orchestration wins — and note that the open question is **how much you build yourself vs. configure in a tool that's catching up**. Dan's own answer ("in ands not ors," ~80% in Claude Code as meta-agent) is the honest resolution. This axis moves fast; date the claim.

---

## Gap 4 — Till-done in the demo vs. the committed `/generate`

**Course-era artifact:** on screen the orchestrator runs a `TillDone` list ([1/8] → [11/11]). The committed `generate.md` carries **no** task list.

**Why it matters:** a reader auditing `generate.md` to "find the till-done logic" won't find it and may think the video is faked.

**Book treatment:** explain the reconciliation once, clearly: `tilldone` is an **orchestrator tool** (declared in `orchestrator.md`), used autonomously for substantial work; `generate.md` deliberately omits a task list per `specs/parallel-team-duplication.md` (a coordination stress-test — "can the orchestrator coordinate three parallel teams from context + trees.yaml + activity.yaml alone?"). Both facts are true.

---

## Gap 5 — The leaf-preview mechanism vs. Dan's on-camera guess

**Course-era artifact:** Dan narrates the previews as "teleport which probably uses iframe underneath."

**Why it matters:** it's an on-the-fly guess, and a reader who trusts it will go hunting for Vue `Teleport` in the preview path.

**Book treatment:** state the real mechanism plainly — a real `<iframe>` (1280×720, CSS-scaled, `pointer-events:none`) into the leaf's gallery route, which uses `import.meta.glob` + a dynamic `<component :is>`; Vue `Teleport` is used only in `Sidebar.vue`. This is a good "read the code, don't trust the narration" teaching beat.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach as durable principles)

These are the load-bearing ideas; none is tied to a tool version:

- **The harness is the leverage point.** Whoever controls context/model/prompt/tools + orchestration — regardless of tool — has the edge. Models commoditize; the harness endures.
- **Solve problem classes, not tasks.** Build teams that operate a whole domain; 80–90% of work is a repeatable workflow.
- **Three tiers with enforced roles.** Orchestrator/leads delegate and don't write; workers do; validators report. Enforce structurally (tools + domain), not by request.
- **One orchestrator interface.** Input must not scale with agent count.
- **Specialization = one agent, one prompt, one purpose,** via expertise + skills + tools + domain (focused context).
- **Agents that keep persistent mental models** — observe, act, learn, iterate; knowledge compounds across sessions.
- **Reliability by design** — heterogeneous, swappable models + redundant teams; a broken worker is survivable.
- **Trust and scale as the north star** — build closed, specialized systems so you can trust them with ever-larger work.
- **Claude Code as meta-agent** — build the system that builds/operates the system; "in ands not ors."

---

## Strict overlay decision (Current-Practice YouTube, map-to-lesson only)

Per the locked plan: overlays must be strict map-to-lesson / named-gap, IndyDevDan's own channel, max 1–3 `include_in_phase1`. This lesson names its own gaps in-video, which makes the choice clean.

**Include in phase 1 (2 cards):**

| ID | Title | maps_to | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `M30gp1315Y4` | Agent Teams (Multi-Team Agentic Coding) | named hole | Dan explicitly links this in-lesson as the video covering the multi-team **harness** UI Agents runs on top of ("we covered that last week... an implementation of the multi-team agent harness"). Fills the single biggest named gap — this lesson *assumes* the harness and only shows an implementation of it. Prerequisite viewing. |
| `TqjmTZRL31E` | Pi CEO Agents | named hole | The first asset in the trilogy (CEO → lead → UI agents) this lesson positions against; Dan references CEO agents for strategic decisions. Grounds the "systems of agents" lineage. |

**Deliberately excluded / not overlays:**
- **Pi Coding Agent (pi.dev)** and **Learn Pi From Zero (github.com/disler/pi-vs-claude-code)** — a tool site and a repo, not videos. List as `reference` resources, not overlays.
- **Claude Code (anthropic.com/claude-code)** — vendor page, reference only.
- **Agentic-security news links** (Autonomous AI Cybercrime, Claude Code RCE, OpenClaw, InversePrompt, Agentic Attack Chains) — third-party context Dan flashes for the Aegis domain; cite as references if the chapter treats the agentic-security angle, but they are not IndyDevDan overlays.

**Cap honored:** exactly 2 `include_in_phase1: true` (≤3). IDs are taken from the lesson's own description reference list (high confidence); **oembed-verify they resolve before publishing links**, exactly as the TAC-1 cross-review did. No 3rd card is added because no additional IndyDevDan video in the reference list maps cleanly to a named hole without topic drift.

# Infinite UI Agents — Lab Spec

**Codebase:** `agentic-horizon-extras/ui-agents` (Agentic Horizon member asset) — the only codebase for this lab. Do **not** use PiCanvas or any other repo.

**Prime directive (the tac ethos):** you don't hand-edit product code. Every change to the system — components, brand, even prompts — is made *by the agents / through the harness*, not by you typing into `index.vue`. Editing **harness config** (front matter, `brand.yaml`, `settings.json`) by hand is allowed and expected; editing generated **product** code by hand is a fail.

### Prerequisites & the two tracks

The full system requires the **Pi coding agent**, the **`teams`** shell alias (from the Multi-Team Agentic Coding member asset), plus `bun`, `node`, `just`, `uv`, and API keys (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; OpenRouter/provider keys only if you attempt the open-source stretch). Because that's member-gated and token-costing, the lab is split:

- **Track A — Read the Harness (Lab 0–1):** fully gradable from the committed files. **No Pi, no `teams`, no API cost.** Everyone can complete and self-grade this from the repo alone.
- **Track B — Run & Specialize the Harness (Lab 2–4):** requires the full member setup and spends tokens. Do this if you have access.

---

## Lab 0 — Setup & orientation (Track A)

1. Open `ui-agents` in your IDE. Run `/install` (via Claude Code) and read what it verifies (Pi + `teams` alias, Bun/Node/just/uv, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, Vue deps, team config, dev-server readiness). You do **not** need every prerequisite to pass Track A.
2. Read `README.md` end to end. Say out loud where you are in the trilogy (**ceo-agents → lead-agents → ui-agents**) and what the tagline demands ("build systems that solve entire problem classes").
3. Read `.pi/settings.json` and state, in one sentence, everything the Pi harness is configured to control here.

**Checkpoint 0 (gradable):** you can name the 4 keys in `settings.json` and what each does (`thinking`, `autoCompact`, `compactThreshold`, `prompts`), and you can state the 5-level hierarchy Brand → Product → Tree → Branch → Leaf without looking.

---

## Lab 1 — Map the harness (Track A, no API cost)

Answer each from the committed files; write your answers down — they are the graded artifact.

**1.1 Count the system.** From `.pi/multi-team/multi-team-config.yaml`: how many teams? How many *unique* agent files in `.pi/multi-team/agents/`? How many total agent *slots* (count A/B/C duplicates)?
> Expected: **8 teams**, **12 unique agent files**, **24 slots** (1 orchestrator + Setup 3 + Brand 2 + UI Gen ×3 + Validation ×3).

**1.2 Prove the tiers.** For `orchestrator.md`, one lead (e.g. `ui-generation-lead.md`), one worker (`vue-generator.md`), and one validator (`hard-validator.md`), record the `tools:` list and the `domain:` permissions.
> Expected: leads/orchestrator have `delegate` + `tilldone`; workers have `write`/`edit`/`bash` (no delegate); validators have neither `write`/`edit` nor `delegate`. Leads' `domain` sets `upsert: false` on `apps/infinite-ui/`; workers set `upsert: true`.

**1.3 Find the enforced rule.** Quote the two lines in `CLAUDE.md` that say leads don't write files and workers do. Explain in one sentence how `tools` + `domain` enforce it structurally.

**1.4 Read the learning loop.** Read `skills/mental-model.md`. In three bullets, state when an agent reads its expertise file, when it updates it, and what it must do after every write (line-count trim + YAML validation).

**1.5 Inspect a mental model.** Open any file in `.pi/multi-team/expertise/`. What's in it? Reconcile with the "7K-token mental model" from the video.
> Expected: a **one-line stub** (`# Mental model — auto-maintained by agent`); the 7,753-token file is runtime state, capped by `max-lines: 10000`.

**1.6 Trace the workflow.** Read `.pi/prompts/multi-team/generate.md`. List its 5 `Variables` and summarize the 8 `Workflow` steps. Where is the "till-done" list in this file?
> Expected: BRAND/PRODUCT/TREE/COUNT/PROMPT; the 8-step Setup→Brand→UIGen→round-robin gen→Setup→round-robin validate→fix→Setup pipeline; **there is no till-done list here** — it's the orchestrator's `tilldone` tool.

**1.7 Prove zero-hardcoded-values.** Open `brands/aegis/products/app/trees/agent-stream/timeline-stack/index.vue`. Find 3 CSS custom properties it uses and locate their source values in `brands/aegis/brand.yaml`. Confirm the leaf uses tokens, not raw hex.

**1.8 Find the preview mechanism.** In `src/canvas/PreviewBranchNode.vue` and `src/gallery/BranchPreview.vue`, identify how a leaf renders. Is it Vue `Teleport`?
> Expected: a real `<iframe>` (1280×720, CSS `transform: scale()`, `pointer-events:none`) → gallery route → `import.meta.glob` + dynamic `<component :is>`. **Not** Teleport (that's only in `Sidebar.vue`).

**Checkpoint 1 (gradable — pass = 7/8 correct):** answers to 1.1–1.8 match the expected values above. This checkpoint requires **no** API spend and certifies you understand the harness before you run it.

---

## Lab 2 — Run the pipeline (Track B, members)

1. `just dev` (starts the Vue app on :5173). `just team` (opens the multi-team chat — you're talking to the Orchestrator).
2. Pick an existing brand/product (`aegis` / `app`) and generate a **new** tree of 3 variants:
   `/generate aegis app pricing 3 "Three pricing-page layouts: a classic 3-tier table, a bold single-plan hero, and a comparison-grid. Use Aegis brand tokens only."`
   (Or use `just generate aegis app pricing 3 "<brief>"`.)
3. Watch the orchestrator delegate: Setup scaffolds → Brand loads context → UI Gen Lead writes 3 briefs → round-robin across UI Generation A/B/C → Validation A/B/C → Setup finalizes. Note the TillDone list appear and advance.
4. When it reports done, `just list-branches aegis app pricing` and browse the results at `/aegis/app` (canvas) and `/aegis/app/gallery/pricing`.

**Checkpoint 2 (gradable) — pass criteria:**
- `trees.yaml` for `aegis/app` shows a `pricing` tree with 3 branches at `status: validated` (or documented `failed` with the reason).
- 3 real `index.vue` leaves exist on disk under `.../pricing/*/index.vue`, each non-stub (> 100 lines) and using **only** brand CSS custom properties (grep for raw `#` hex in `<style>` → none outside `:root`/token declarations).
- All 3 render in the browser gallery and are visually on-brand for Aegis.
- **You typed zero lines of Vue by hand.** Every component came from the team.

---

## Lab 3 — Specialize the harness (Track B, members)

1. **Retarget an agent (edit front matter, not code).** In `vue-generator.md`, tighten `domain` to a single product path (e.g. `apps/infinite-ui/src/brands/aegis/products/site/`) and re-run a generation scoped there. Observe that the agent stays in its lane.
2. **Live rebrand (through the Brand team).** Run `/rebrand aegis "shift the accent from crimson to amber; keep everything else"` (or edit `aegis/brand.yaml` by hand — harness config edit, allowed) and watch every rendered component update live via CSS custom properties. Do **not** edit any `index.vue`.
3. **Watch a mental model grow.** Before and after a generation run, `wc -l` an agent's `expertise/*.yaml`. Confirm it moved from the 1-line stub toward populated, self-authored entries.

**Checkpoint 3 (gradable) — pass criteria:**
- The retargeted agent wrote **only** inside its narrowed `domain` (verify via `git status` / paths touched).
- The rebrand changed the rendered UI **without** any hand-edit to a leaf (`git diff` shows changes only in `brand.yaml`, not in `index.vue` files).
- At least one `expertise/*.yaml` is no longer a 1-line stub after your run.

---

## Lab 4 — Stretch (Track B, members)

- **S1 — Reproduce the reliability lesson.** Assign an open-source model to one team's worker in front matter (e.g. `model: openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.7` on a `vue-generator` instance) and re-run `/generate`. Observe whether the worker underperforms or fails — and whether its lead / another team picks up the work. Then restore Sonnet and rerun. Write 3 sentences on what this teaches about model choice and redundancy.
- **S2 — Compose a new command against the team.** Add a reusable prompt in `.pi/prompts/multi-team/` (follow the `generate.md` shape: frontmatter → Purpose → Variables → Instructions → Workflow → Report). E.g. `/audit <brand> <product>` that delegates a brand-compliance sweep to the Brand + Validation teams. Prove it runs from `just`/`teams`.
- **S3 — Fork a leaf.** `/fork-leaf aegis app agent-stream compact-dashboard 2 "one denser, one calmer"`. Confirm the 2 forks carry `forkedFrom` in `trees.yaml` and attach to their parent branch on the canvas.
- **S4 — Read the meta-layer.** In `.claude/skills/drive/`, read how the tmux `drive` skill (`session`/`run`/`poll`/`fanout`/`screenshot`) is used to script and record the `teams` chat. In one paragraph, explain how Dan drove/recorded the demo — the Claude-Code-as-meta-agent layer.

---

## Final pass sheet

You pass the lab if:

- **[Track A]** Checkpoint 0 and Checkpoint 1 are complete (≥7/8 on Lab 1), with written answers matching the expected values — **achieved with zero API spend.**
- **[Track A]** You can state, without notes: the six harness components; the three tiers and who writes files; the four front-matter specialization fields (and why `domain` matters); and the committed-vs-demo divergence (all-Sonnet, empty stubs, one brand).
- **[Track B, if attempted]** Checkpoint 2 met: 3 validated, on-brand, browseable leaves generated **by the team**, zero hand-written Vue.
- **[Track B, if attempted]** Checkpoint 3 met: a retargeted agent stayed in its `domain`, a rebrand changed the UI without touching any leaf, and a mental model grew past its stub.
- **Prime directive honored throughout:** no hand-edited product code; all product changes came from the agents.

---

## Instructor notes & guardrails

- **Grade Track A from artifacts, not vibes.** The Lab 1 answers are objective (counts, tool lists, file contents) and checkable against the repo. This is the equalizer for readers without member access or API budget.
- **Token economics (Track B).** A single `/generate ... 3` run drives ~8–11 delegated tasks across up to 6 teams — it is not cheap. Budget for it; watch the per-agent cost/token telemetry in the `teams` chat (the demo hit ~$6.70 / 29 min for one 3-variant run at full scale).
- **Expect failures, and grade them as data.** If a worker stalls, the correct behavior is the lead covering or a sibling team completing the branch — that *is* the reliability lesson. Document failures with their reason rather than treating them as a lab-breaking error.
- **Don't hunt for Teleport.** Steer students to the real preview path (`iframe` + `import.meta.glob`); it's a deliberate "read the code, not the narration" beat.
- **Guardrails.** Don't improvise destructive git commands. Keep generation scoped to `aegis` (or a fresh `/new-brand`) so runs stay reproducible. Restore any front-matter/model edits after stretch exercises so the base config is clean for the next reader.
